What if the feature misbehaves after launch?
We set a switch that turns it off or back to a fallback in one step, and we test it before launch. During the order period we fix issues as they appear. Later problems fall under ongoing support.
Do you need to build the feature first?
No. If it already exists, we launch it. If we built it, we use what we know. If someone else did, we review it first and tell you what needs fixing before it goes live.
Can you tell my customers about it?
Yes. We can draft a short announcement for your site or email and add a simple notice that explains the AI feature. You approve the wording before anything goes out.

desc:
Launch and support for your AI feature takes it from tested to live in a controlled way. Ecom Swift LLC prepares a checklist, releases to a small group first, watches the early answers and errors, and fixes what shows up, so real users meet a feature that has already been checked.

## What does an AI launch involve?

An AI launch is the set of steps between a feature that works in testing and one that real customers or staff rely on. It covers final checks on live settings, a plan for switching the feature on, a way to switch it off again, monitoring of what it says, and preparing the people who will deal with questions.

Launching an AI feature differs from launching a normal page. Its output is not fixed. The same question can produce different wording on different days, and real users ask things nobody tested.

## Why a staged release is safer

Testing uses questions that the team can imagine. Real users are more creative. They paste long documents, ask about competitors, use slang and test the limits. A release to everyone on day one exposes all of them at once, including to any mistake you have not found.

A staged release starts small. A limited group uses the feature, you read what happened, fix the weak spots and then widen access. If something goes wrong, fewer people see it, and you have a prepared way back.

## How a good launch affects the outcome

A careful launch protects trust. People forgive a limited feature that admits uncertainty. They are less forgiving of a confident wrong answer in public. Monitoring in the first days catches patterns early, such as a topic the feature handles badly or an error that appears only on certain devices.

It also gives your staff confidence. When support teams know what the feature does and how to escalate, they handle questions calmly instead of discovering problems from angry messages.

## What a good launch includes

- A launch checklist covering settings, limits, content, wording and ownership.
- A final test on the live configuration, not only on a test copy.
- A clear switch-on plan and a written rollback plan.
- A release to a small group before everyone.
- A daily review of answers and error logs during launch week.
- An alert when answers fail or look odd.
- A set of quick fixes made in response to what the first users do.
- A feedback button, so users can flag a poor answer in one tap.
- A short guide and briefing for staff and support teams.
- A written plan for what to watch and improve after launch.

## What we do

We begin with a review of the feature you have built, whether we built it or someone else did. We check the live settings, confirm limits and agree who owns each decision. Then we run the release in steps and review real use as it comes in.

The Basic package covers the checklist, a final live test, switch-on and rollback plans and a staff guide. The Standard package adds a staged release, daily checks, a set of quick fixes, alerts and a staff briefing. The Premium package adds a three-step rollout, more fixes, a feedback button, a usage and quality report, a support team briefing and a written next-steps plan. Ongoing monthly tuning is quoted separately.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Name one person who can switch the feature off.
- Release first to people who will report problems honestly.
- Read real conversations, not only summary charts.
- Tell users plainly what the feature can and cannot do.
- Keep a list of fixes and the reason for each.

**Avoid:**
- Launching on a busy sales day with no time to watch it.
- Changing several settings at once, so the cause of a problem is unclear.
- Assuming silence means everything is fine.
- Leaving staff to find out about the feature from customers.
- Skipping the rollback plan because it feels unlikely to be needed.

## Who it is for

A team has finished testing a customer assistant and wants a safe first week. A store owner is about to switch on an AI helper before a promotion. A company with an in-house tool wants an outside check before staff rely on it.

## What we need from you

We need access to the feature and its settings as a collaborator, team or developer user where the platform supports it, the names of the people who will own it and a date window for release. We never need passwords. If the feature is not built yet, we recommend starting with the build or testing service first.
